summary: The note explains absolute zero as the lowest limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale, defined as 0 K (−273.15 °C, −459.67 °F), where a cooled ideal gas reaches minimum enthalpy and entropy. It covers why absolute zero cannot be reached by thermodynamic means, the thermodynamic behavior near 0 K (third law, Nernst postulate, perfect crystals), Bose–Einstein condensates, negative temperatures, the historical search for absolute zero from Boyle and Amontons through Kelvin, Dewar and Kamerlingh Onnes, and record low temperatures achieved in labs and space.
one_line: Absolute zero is the lowest limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale (0 K, −273.15 °C), its theory, historical discovery, and the record cold temperatures reached near it.
key_facts: Absolute zero is taken as −273.15 degrees Celsius, which equals −459.67 degrees Fahrenheit, by international agreement.

The laws of thermodynamics indicate that absolute zero cannot be reached using only thermodynamic means, because the temperature of the cooled substance approaches the temperature of the cooling agent asymptotically.
Max Planck's strong form of the third law of thermodynamics states the entropy of a perfect crystal vanishes at absolute zero.
The Fermi temperature for typical electron densities found in metals is on the order of 80,000 K.
A Bose–Einstein condensate was first produced in 1995 by Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman at the University of Colorado at Boulder NIST-JILA lab, using rubidium atoms cooled to 170 nanokelvin.
A record cold temperature of 450 ± 80 picokelvin was achieved in a BEC of sodium atoms in 2003 by researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.
Bose and Einstein predicted the Bose–Einstein condensate state of matter in 1924–25.
Robert Boyle's 1665 New Experiments and Observations touching Cold articulated the dispute known as the primum frigidum.
Guillaume Amontons first addressed the question of a limit to coldness in 1703, and his zero was equivalent to about −240 on the Celsius scale.
In 1848 Lord Kelvin devised a scale of absolute temperature whose zero was placed at approximately −273 °C.
In 1908 Heike Kamerlingh Onnes was the first to liquefy helium, reaching the boiling point of helium at −269 °C (4.15 K), and his achievement earned him the Nobel Prize in 1913.
The average temperature of the universe today is approximately 2.73 kelvins, based on measurements of cosmic microwave background radiation.
The Boomerang Nebula has a temperature of 1 K, the lowest observed outside of a laboratory.
In September 2014, CUORE collaboration scientists cooled a copper vessel of one cubic meter to 0.006 kelvins for 15 days at the Laboratori Nazionali del Gran Sasso in Italy.
The current world record for effective temperatures was set in 2021 at 38 picokelvin through matter-wave lensing of rubidium Bose–Einstein condensates.

entities.name: Absolute zero
entities.role: lowest limit of the thermodynamic temperature scale, taken as zero kelvin

entities.name: Bose–Einstein condensate
entities.role: state of matter of a dilute gas of weakly interacting bosons cooled very near absolute zero

entities.role: co-predictor of the Bose–Einstein condensate state of matter in 1924–25

entities.role: extended Bose's ideas to material particles and translated Bose's paper for publication

entities.role: produced the first gaseous condensate in 1995 with Carl Wieman

entities.role: produced the first gaseous condensate in 1995 with Eric Cornell

entities.role: researchers achieved a record cold BEC of sodium atoms in 2003

entities.name: Guillaume Amontons

entities.name: Johann Heinrich Lambert

entities.name: Lord Kelvin
entities.role: devised in 1848 a scale of absolute temperature independent of any particular substance
